objections.front: Gallio and Erastus — why does the essay insist on being exact about what each stone shows?
objections.back: The Delphi inscription dates the official, not the apostle; it is the synchronism with Acts 18:12 that anchors Paul at Corinth. The Erastus pavement may name the man Paul greets in Romans 16:23, but the identification is plausible rather than secure, since the office is not a clean match for Paul’s Greek term.

objections.front: Why does the exact title on the Pilate Stone matter?
objections.back: It names him prefect of Judea — the correct title in Pilate’s own day. Later Roman writers anachronistically called him “procurator,” a title not introduced until Claudius, while the Gospels’ generic “governor” is consistent with the stone.

objections.front: “The orthodoxy test is circular — they kept the books that already agreed with them.”
objections.back: The rule of faith was not drawn up to fit a list: it is a short summary of the apostolic preaching, attested around AD 180 independently of any list, and it names no books. And the criteria had teeth — the church kept Revelation, Hebrews, and 2 Peter through long doubt. This does not prove the criterion infallible; it shows the criterion did not decide the outcome.

objections.front: Why does Irenaeus’s “four winds” argument for exactly four Gospels count as evidence?
objections.back: It is a strange-sounding argument to modern ears, but it only works if, around AD 180, a fourfold Gospel was already an established fact his readers would not dispute.

objections.front: Why is the early-fourth-century sorting into “recognized,” “disputed,” and “spurious” books decisive?
objections.back: Because it comes before Nicaea: a careful sorting by inherited usage was already underway before Constantine’s council met. That is the decisive evidence against the conspiracy story.

objections.front: A critic says John invented Philip’s hometown to fit the feeding’s location. Your reply?
objections.back: John’s own feeding scene never names Bethsaida, and Philip’s hometown sits five chapters earlier in a disciple-list, with no signal pointing forward. An inventor cashes in his invention; he does not bury the one detail that makes it pay. The alternative is available in principle but far less economical than that John simply knew it.

objections.front: A critic says the author of Acts simply mined Paul’s letters. Your reply?
objections.back: Dependence has not been ruled out, but Acts does not behave like a document built out of the letters: it never verbatim-quotes them and diverges where a borrower would lean on his source — suggestive rather than decisive. The real weight falls on the shape of the agreements: harmonizers connect the dots; these texts leave them unconnected.

objections.front: What does the literary-dependence objection rightly force a defender to concede?
objections.back: That where a coincidence holds only between texts in a known dependence relation — especially Mark and a Gospel that used Mark — redaction is a live alternative and such cases carry less weight. A defender cannot simply wave away Markan priority, the majority view; McGrew herself treats cases as having different strengths and sets aside ones too weak to lean on.

objections.front: Why doesn’t redaction explain the strongest cases?
objections.back: When a later author notices a connection in his source, the natural editorial move is to state it. The strong cases do the opposite: the explaining detail sits in a different document, dropped for an unrelated reason, with neither writer flagging the link. And the strongest cross-Gospel cases draw the explaining detail from a Gospel not in the relevant source relation.

objections.front: Why is the Philip-and-Bethsaida case among the cleanest?
objections.back: John alone has Jesus ask Philip where to buy bread; Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida; and John, chapters earlier and for an unrelated reason, notes Philip was from Bethsaida. The explaining detail sits in a different part of John, the geographical anchor comes from a different Gospel altogether — and no Gospel draws the link.

objections.front: Why should the “green grass” case be held loosely?
objections.back: Mark’s green grass and John’s nearby Passover cohere, since the grass is green only briefly in spring. But this is where the literary-dependence objection bites hardest: if John knew Mark, he could have inferred the season from Mark, so the case should be conceded as weak if John used Mark and dropped from the load-bearing cases.

objections.front: Why would four perfectly matching accounts be a worse sign, not a better one?
objections.back: Independent testimony to a real event almost never lines up perfectly; perfect alignment would smell of collusion. Accounts that differ on incidentals but converge on a core show the pattern of substantially independent witnesses.

objections.argName: The Dead Sea Scrolls and Old Testament Reliability
objections.front: How does the argument answer “standardization involved choices your measurement cannot see”?
objections.back: It narrows the claim without defeating it. The Scrolls illuminate the period after a proto-Masoretic text emerged better than its prehistory, but the argument only has to answer the charge of corruption across the documented centuries — and the standardization choices are now visible precisely because the Scrolls preserved the alternatives.

objections.argName: The Dead Sea Scrolls and Old Testament Reliability
objections.front: What is pluriformity — and why must the honest apologist concede it?
objections.back: Before standardization, largely complete by the end of the first century AD, the biblical books circulated in more than one textual form at once. Conceding it is the price of telling the truth: the slogan that the Scrolls prove the Bible never changed is false as stated.

objections.argName: The Dead Sea Scrolls and Old Testament Reliability
objections.front: Why does the breadth of the Qumran library matter?
objections.back: Fragments of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther (and, on most counts, Nehemiah, though that identification is debated) are among more than two hundred biblical scrolls. That is a whole library, not one lucky survival — a real cross-section of the text centuries before the medieval Masoretes.

objections.argName: The Dead Sea Scrolls and Old Testament Reliability
objections.front: Why does the size of the proto-Masoretic group matter?
objections.back: Tov’s own data show it was already the largest group at Qumran — roughly half the scrolls by his third-edition tallies. So the medieval Masoretic Text was not a late, drifting invention but the faithful descendant of a text already fixed in essentials a thousand years earlier.

objections.argName: The Dead Sea Scrolls and Old Testament Reliability
objections.front: Why is “preservation is not truth” the line that governs the whole argument?
objections.back: Because the Scrolls address transmission, not truth: they cannot show that the Red Sea parted or that Isaiah’s prophecies came from God. What they remove is the charge that the text is too garbled to know what it originally said, so the arguments about its contents can proceed on a stable text.

objections.argName: The Early Date of the New Testament
objections.front: Why does the creed’s early date cross ideological lines — and what caution goes with the survey figure?
objections.back: The tradition must predate Paul’s Jerusalem meeting with two of its named witnesses three years after his conversion, and even a scholar who rejects a bodily resurrection dates its elements to “the first two years after the crucifixion… not later than three years.” The survey of scholarly support is a count of published positions assembled by one researcher, not a randomized poll, and should be cited with care.

objections.argName: The Early Date of the New Testament
objections.front: Why does the mainstream date Mark around AD 70 — and is that special pleading?
objections.back: Matthew and Luke used Mark as a source, so Mark circulated first, and Mark 13’s prediction of Jerusalem’s destruction is read as written after the event. It is not special pleading as a method — historians as a rule do not assume genuine foreknowledge when an ordinary explanation is available — but the inference is far less decisive than it sounds.

objections.argName: The Early Date of the New Testament
objections.front: Why is the after-the-fact reading of Mark 13 less decisive than it sounds?
objections.back: The prediction is conspicuously unspecific — nothing of the fire, the months-long siege or Titus’s legions — and its most vivid imagery is drawn from Scripture, not from the events of 70. Nor does predicting the Temple’s fall require foreknowledge to be early: Josephus reports another Jesus crying woe on the city and sanctuary from AD 62, years before the war.

objections.argName: The Reliability of the Gospel Eyewitnesses
objections.front: Memory drifts. Why doesn’t that sink the argument?
objections.back: The studies that show memory failing typically involve fleeting, peripheral events witnessed once; memory is far more durable for repeated, salient, emotionally central experiences. And the eyewitnesses were still alive, often leading the movement, while the tradition formed — a brake on legend, not its engine.

objections.argName: The Reliability of the Gospel Eyewitnesses
objections.front: What does the earliest external witness report about Mark — and why doesn’t a later historian’s disdain for him sink it?
objections.back: That Mark, having become Peter’s interpreter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, what Peter remembered — a tradition Papias traced to “the Elder.” Eusebius’s disdain was aimed chiefly at Papias’s millenarian eschatology rather than at his reliability about Mark, and what Papias passes on is not his own speculation.

objections.argName: The Reliability of the Gospel Eyewitnesses
objections.front: Why does Mark bother to name a walk-on character’s sons?
objections.back: Mark 15:21 names Simon of Cyrene as the father of Alexander and Rufus. The economical explanation is that they were known figures in the community for whom Mark wrote — the named guarantors of a story their father had lived. An inference, not a proof, but a better explanation of an odd habit than the form critics offered.

objections.argName: The Argument from the Jewishness of Jesus
objections.front: “passages like Matthew 22:7 show the Gospels are post-war documents.”
objections.back: Grant that some Gospels were finished, and in places shaped, after 70 — which most of the field holds. But late shaping can add an anachronism; it does not supply the large body of accurate pre-war, Palestinian detail. A late hand explains a late fingerprint; it does not explain why the rest of the prints are early.

objections.argName: The Argument from the Jewishness of Jesus
objections.front: Why does the pre-70 detail matter against later invention?
objections.back: The Gospels assume a functioning Temple, a working priesthood, live Pharisee–Sadducee disputes, and a village map of pre-war Galilee — a world the war of 66–70 swept away. A later author reconstructing it from books would be prone to anachronism; the Gospels get it right in passing. A probabilistic, comparative judgment, not a proof.

objections.argName: The Argument from the Jewishness of Jesus
objections.front: Why would a free inventor have made Jesus less Jewish, not more?
objections.back: The Gospels circulated in a church rapidly becoming Gentile and increasingly in tension with the synagogue; an inventor there had every reason to smooth away the embarrassments and universalize the figure. Instead the tradition keeps sayings awkward for a Gentile mission, such as “only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24).

objections.front: What does the leading skeptic concede?
objections.back: In a written exchange appended to later editions of Misquoting Jesus, Bart Ehrman agrees with Bruce Metzger “that the essential Christian beliefs are not affected by textual variants,” and says a jointly reconstructed text would differ in “maybe one or two dozen places out of many thousands.” The under-one-percent figure is Wallace’s, not Ehrman’s.

objections.front: Why does the argument survive if P75 is dated later?
objections.back: Its date rests on paleography and carries real uncertainty, but the argument turns on how carefully it was copied — it is the exemplar of the Alands’ “strict text” — not on the exact decade. The honest form is narrow: other early papyri, such as P66 and P45, are classed “free.”

objections.front: Why is the raw count of Greek manuscripts not itself the argument?
objections.back: The great majority of those Greek copies are later, medieval manuscripts. The weight lies in the early witnesses and their wide geographic spread, not in sheer number.

objections.front: Why is the variant count not news — and how was it first answered?
objections.back: In 1707 John Mill’s Greek New Testament catalogued some 30,000 variants; in 1713 the deist Anthony Collins argued they left the text uncertain, and Richard Bentley answered him the same year that the true text is not lost but dispersed among the copies. The abundance of variants is a function of the abundance of witnesses.

objections.front: Answer Tuckett’s objection in one move.
objections.back: Grant the logic and narrow the claim: the names cannot by themselves prove that a Galilean fisherman wrote them down. But a “skilled diaspora mimic” would need the relative frequencies and the nicknaming right across dozens of incidental characters, with no tables to work from — Tuckett shows the door is not bolted, not that anyone of the relevant profile walked through it.

objections.front: What tool did no ancient author have — and why does its absence matter?
objections.back: Name-frequency tables. Without them no ancient author could ensure the second-commonest name appeared about as often as it actually did, or that rare names stayed rare in roughly the right proportion. The pattern can leak out of genuine memory; it is very hard to engineer from the outside.

objections.front: Why does a forger’s own background count against him?
objections.back: The diaspora profile differed sharply, with far more Greek names. A diaspora writer would not merely fail to copy the Palestinian list; he would tend to default to the names of his own world — his background actively pulls him away from the watermark.

objections.argName: The Argument from Fulfilled Prophecy in the Old Testament
objections.front: Doesn’t “You are my servant, Israel” (Isaiah 49:3) settle that the Servant is the nation?
objections.back: No: two verses later this Servant is formed “to bring Jacob back to him,” so a Servant named Israel has a mission to Israel and cannot simply be the nation as a whole. The verdict is bounded — it does not prove the Servant is the Messiah, and the remnant reading remains an option — but it removes 49:3 as proof that “the Servant” always means the nation.

objections.argName: The Argument from Fulfilled Prophecy in the Old Testament
objections.front: Isaiah 53 is about the nation of Israel.
objections.back: Within the song the servant suffers for the people and is distinguished from “my people” (53:8), and he “had done no violence” (53:9), while servant-Israel elsewhere in Isaiah is “blind” and “deaf” and is told, “you have burdened me with your sins.” Defenders of the collective reading appeal to a righteous remnant, and the referent is genuinely contested — but the individual reading is the better one, and Jesus fits it.

objections.argName: The Argument from Fulfilled Prophecy in the Old Testament
objections.front: The evangelists invented the passion story out of the Old Testament.
objections.back: Concede that they shaped their narratives with Scripture in view. But the crucifixion under Pilate — which Crossan himself grants — is reported by a Roman and a Jewish historian, not derived from any psalm; a crucified messiah was not a story first-century Jews were predisposed to invent; and a broad center of scholarship judges the passion tradition “history scripturalized,” not “prophecy historicized.” As an account of how the passion narrative arose, the objection fails: the narrative has a remembered core, and the question is only how far Scripture shaped its telling.

objections.argName: The Argument from Fulfilled Prophecy in the Old Testament
objections.front: The prophecies are as elastic as horoscopes.
objections.back: Concede the point for the loose texts and decline to use them. Vagueness is a real defect of some alleged prophecies; it is not a feature of “born in Bethlehem,” “buried with a rich man,” or “garments divided by lot.” A case that quietly drops its weak members is not weakened; it is disciplined.

objections.argName: The Argument from Fulfilled Prophecy in the Old Testament
objections.front: Why is the popular statistical case for prophecy retired?
objections.back: Assigning a numerical probability to “born in Bethlehem” requires guesses dressed as data, and the multiplication assumes the events are independent when they plainly are not. Its pseudo-precision gives critics an easy target and substitutes arithmetic for argument; the real case — convergence, not arithmetic — does not need it, and is stronger without it.

objections.front: A critic grants that Christ preexisted but calls him a subordinate heavenly being. What is the dispute really about — and how far does this case answer it?
objections.back: The dispute is one of kind, not date: not whether the preexistent figure is early, but what rank he holds. This case answers it in part: Paul makes Christ the one through whom all things were made, and the one by whom every created thing was made cannot himself be one of the created things. The fuller case is taken up in the divine-identity essays.

objections.front: “The creation language is just Wisdom-poetry, not a preexistent person.”
objections.back: Concede that Wisdom-personification is a genuine part of the background. But Wisdom in Proverbs is a poetic personification of an attribute of God; Paul’s Christ is a person with a name, who is “sent,” who “became poor,” who was crucified and raised — a biography, not a personified quality. The motif illuminates the creation language; it does not dissolve the personal subject who undergoes the descent.

objections.front: Why does “he became poor” point to a prior state?
objections.back: The logic is a transition: he was rich, and became poor. A man who was born poor did not “become” poor for anyone’s sake; the sentence presupposes a wealth held before the becoming. It faces its own skeptical reading — a metaphor of earthly self-impoverishment — which is why the case is cumulative.

objections.front: Why does the order of Galatians 4:4 matter — and what is its limit?
objections.back: God sent his Son, and the Son was then “born of woman.” The sending is named before the birth, which reads awkwardly if the sending simply is the birth of an ordinary man. Limit: taken alone, “sent” need not imply preexistence — prophets are “sent” too — so the weight falls on the cumulative pattern.

objections.front: Why is morphē the hinge of Philippians 2:6–7?
objections.back: The same noun describes what he became — a servant — and his servanthood was no costume, so the “form of God” he began in is equally real. And the sequence — in the form of God, then a servant’s form, then born in human likeness — describes a transition from one condition to another.

objections.front: “it’s just evolved human empathy — no God needed.”
objections.back: Part of it plausibly is — reciprocity and kin loyalty pay, so nature can produce them. But the conviction at issue goes further than anything reciprocity explains: that the useless stranger, the enemy, the child who can never repay you has equal and inviolable worth — which is exactly what Nietzsche saw runs against selection, not with it. And even if empathy were wholly evolved, that only describes a feeling we happen to have; it would not tell us the weak ought to be protected. That move needs a standard evolution cannot supply.

objections.front: “plenty of ancient people were compassionate too.”
objections.back: Granted, and the claim survives all of it: individual pagans loved their children and the Stoics reasoned movingly about a shared humanity. But the point is narrower — no Greek or Roman society rested a law, movement, or institution on the conviction that the weak, as the weak, have first claim on the strong simply by being human. Care flowed toward the useful. Israel stands apart, and is the root: its law already commanded care for the widow, the orphan and the stranger.

objections.front: “the church’s good record proves Christianity is true.”
objections.back: No — the argument refuses that inference. A belief system can remake the world for the better and still be false, so the social record is no knock-down proof of a creed, and that case rests above all on the resurrection. But it is not nothing: the moral vision even the unbeliever lives by is hard to ground in a universe with no God behind it (some hold it needs none, as a brute fact; the Christian answers that a moral source explains it better). The record shows where a conviction came from — not that the creed is true.

objections.front: The image of God — whose doctrine is it, and why does the pedigree matter?
objections.back: It is a Jewish doctrine (Genesis 1:26–27), older than the church and standing on its own feet — the root, shared with Judaism, that Christianity carried into the Gentile world. It matters because worth is conferred by the Creator, not earned by usefulness, so it cannot be forfeited by weakness: the measure of a person is no longer what he can do but whose image he bears.

objections.front: Why is care for the weak “as the weak” called historically rare rather than natural?
objections.back: Because for most of recorded history most people did not believe it, and the civilisations that gave us geometry, tragedy and philosophy emphatically did not. Care flowed toward the strong and the useful; a newborn had to qualify as “worth rearing”; the infirmaries served soldiers and valuable slaves. The idea that a human has a claim on you precisely when he can give nothing back would have struck a thoughtful Roman not as obvious but as perverse.

objections.front: Why is the genocidal turn not something nature itself forbids?
objections.back: Because nature, described simply as nature, can tell you what survives but cannot tell you survival is good, or that the weak may or may not be discarded. Once the premise that man is merely part of nature is treated as a command rather than a description, nothing within nature forbids where it can be taken — the direction Heinrich Himmler took (“man is nothing special at all,” cited only to show where the premise leads, the conclusion this track refuses). To forbid the atrocity you need a value that stands above nature. (Logic, not biography: Nietzsche himself despised anti-Semitism and did not take that step.)

objections.front: “‘He became a curse for us’ makes God a divine child-abuser.”
objections.back: It targets one crude version of one theory of the atonement, not the shared confession — and misreads even that. On classical Christian teaching the one who “became a curse for us” is not a third party the Father abuses but God himself, the eternal Son, willingly giving himself: “in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). It never means the Father hated the Son, nor that the divine nature could die or be cursed.

objections.front: How does the New Testament answer the curse — and what does it not mean?
objections.back: Through the offending text itself: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13, quoting Deuteronomy 21:23). The curse was real, and it was borne, willingly, in the place of those who deserved it — the scandal absorbed and turned inside out. It never means that the Father hated or was divided from the Son, nor that the divine nature could die or be cursed.

objections.front: Why is the scandal of the cross evidence rather than a weakness?
objections.back: Inventors do not sabotage their own inventions. A group fabricating a messianic hero, or gilding the memory of a beloved teacher, has every reason to leave out the detail that most discredits the claim — and crucifixion was that detail. Placing it at the dead center of the preaching is what looks like a community stuck with a fact it could not deny and did not choose.

objections.front: Some ancient voices reached toward a common humanity. Why doesn’t that sink Premise 2?
objections.back: Because two things are true of them: they grounded common humanity in a shared nature rather than in a worth bestowed on each, and — decisively — none became a movement, a law, or a settled conviction. Seneca kept his slaves; Ulpian’s maxim sat inside a code that enforced slavery. The dissent lived as an idea and never became anything more.

objections.front: Why is equal worth a value and not a measurement?
objections.back: Because as a measurement it is plainly false: people differ in every capacity you can weigh, count or test — nothing comes out equal. “Equal worth” is a claim about what a person is, laid over a mass of evidence that they are not equal in what they can do. Its feeling of obviousness is itself the thing to explain.

objections.front: Why is the image of God credited to Judaism, not treated as a Christian invention?
objections.back: Because the doctrine that every human bears God’s image developed in Jewish scripture and Jewish interpretation and stands on its own feet: Genesis says God made humanity, male and female alike, in his own image, so worth is conferred, not earned, and identical in each. The church did not invent it — what it did was carry it into the Gentile world at scale.

objections.front: “Isaiah 52:13 and 6:1 share a phrase, not a meaning” — what is granted, and why does the argument stand?
objections.back: Granted: nothing claims that Isaiah intended a cross; the reading-together mechanism is a reconstruction; “high and lifted up” is used of proud men. But in Isaiah 2 that human loftiness is exactly what the LORD humbles — which makes the Servant’s exaltation in the throne-vision’s words more striking, not less. And the argument does not stand on the echo: John, the Philippians hymn and Revelation 5 make the same pairing of humiliation and divine worship. The verbal echo is corroboration; the convergence of witnesses is the case.

objections.front: Why does the angel who refuses worship sharpen Revelation 5?
objections.back: In the very same book an angel twice refuses the worship John offers and redirects it to God (19:10; 22:8–9); the Lamb receives it without a word of protest. And the Lamb is not worshiped in spite of the wounds. He is identified by them: the figure who shares the worship of the Creator is the slaughtered one.

objections.front: “The man Christ Jesus” is from the disputed Pastorals, so drop it.
objections.back: Concede the disputed authorship; nothing in the case depends on it. Galatians 4:4, Romans 8:3, 1 Corinthians 15, and the humanity of the Philippians hymn are in the undisputed letters, and Hebrews and the Gospels stand outside the Pastorals question. Remove them and the case is unweakened.

objections.front: Why is Paul’s assuming the humanity, rather than arguing it, strong evidence?
objections.back: Because a thing presupposed offhandedly by a writer making some other point was not up for debate. And it comes from the oldest datable Christian documents we possess, earlier than any of the Gospels.

objections.front: Jesus didn’t finish the Messiah’s work, so he’s disqualified.
objections.back: Ask in what order the prophets place these things. Isaiah’s Servant is “despised and rejected” and “poured out his soul to death” before he “prolongs his days” (53). A test that rules out any claimant who “was killed” is stricter than the prophets themselves. The New Testament claims two comings (Acts 3:21; Hebrews 9:28): the sin-bearing first, the peace at his return. This removes the disqualification; it does not by itself prove he is the Messiah.

objections.front: The Servant of Isaiah 53 is the nation Israel.
objections.back: Within the song the Servant suffers “for the transgression of my people” — distinct from the people — and is innocent, where servant-Israel elsewhere is “blind” and “deaf”; in 49:5–6 he restores Jacob. The individual reading is ancient (Targum 52:13). Hold it gently: the collective reading is sincere and was sharpened under Christian persecution. The referent is contested, but the objection does not hold, and Jesus fits the individual reading.

objections.front: Why can’t Isaiah 53 have been written after Jesus?
objections.back: The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran contains all of chapter 53 and is dated by paleography and radiocarbon to roughly 125 BC — over a century before Jesus — in substantially the text behind modern Bibles. No one shaped Isaiah after the fact.

objections.front: What is the honest hedge on Kyrios as the rendering of YHWH — and why does the argument survive it?
objections.back: What the earliest Greek copies wrote, and what was said aloud, is genuinely debated: several pre-Christian copies preserve the Tetragrammaton rather than Kyrios. But the load-bearing fact is what the New Testament writers do on the page: where the Hebrew has YHWH they write Kyrios, and they apply that passage to Jesus.

objections.front: Why does it matter that 1 Corinthians 8:6 sits in an argument against idolatry?
objections.back: Because smuggling in a second divine power would be the very sin Paul is condemning. Set against the pagan world’s many “gods” and many “lords,” his “one God … one Lord” distributes the Shema’s two words for the one God rather than adding a second deity — a reading that is influential and genuinely contested.

objections.front: Why does the case not rest on the Hebrew word echad?
objections.back: Because the “compound unity” argument proves far less than its enthusiasts suppose: the plurality in “one flesh” comes from the noun, not from echad, which is simply the ordinary Hebrew numeral “one” and routinely describes things that are emphatically singular. The case rests on something much harder to wave away: what the New Testament writers actually do with the divine name.

objections.front: Why is the choice of Isaiah 45 so telling?
objections.back: Because it is one of the most fiercely monotheistic chapters in all of Scripture — “I am the LORD, and there is no other.” To take the chapter that most insists there is no god beside the LORD and apply its exclusive oath to Jesus is not to add a second, lesser lord to the picture; it is to say that the one who bears this name is the LORD.

objections.front: The messianic secret — what is sound in it, and why does the theory fail?
objections.back: Sound: Mark’s Jesus often commands silence. But the commands are not one thing — many concern healings, and those do not work as concealment; much messianic material is public (a blind man’s “Son of David,” the entry, the temple, the trial); and the real reticence has a better explanation — “Messiah” was a dangerous word. Mark has certainly shaped the secrecy motif, and nothing rests on any one command being historical. The theory explains the secrecy only by leaving the cross unexplained.

objections.front: Why does “The King of the Jews” read like a Roman formula, not a church confession?
objections.back: Christians called him Christ and Lord. In the Gospels the phrase is on outsiders’ lips; where Jews speak for themselves they say “King of Israel.” And Rome treated such a claim as sedition: a band of rebels that found a leader made him king at once. Pilate’s charge places Jesus, in Rome’s eyes, in that category, though he had raised no army.

objections.front: Why is Easter alone very hard to make the source of the title “Messiah”?
objections.back: In the categories of the time a resurrection, by itself, would mark a vindicated martyr, not a Messiah; nothing in our sources treats rising from the dead as the Messiah’s sign. So the title is very hard to derive from Easter alone. The apostles read Easter as God’s confirmation — but a confirmation needs something to confirm. And they kept the hardest claim: a crucified Messiah.

objections.front: Why is the donkey entry weak evidence of fulfilled prophecy but strong evidence of a claim?
objections.back: Because the Gospels present Jesus as deliberately arranging it. A staged fulfilment proves no prediction — but a man who arranges to ride into the city of David on Zechariah’s pattern before Passover pilgrims is acting out his self-understanding. The argument needs only that he chose the gesture, not that the scene was large.

objections.front: Why is the reply to John a claim rather than an evasion?
objections.back: He answers with the signs Isaiah foretold and invokes them as his credential; a pre-Christian Jewish text already named an anointed one beside those deeds. The reply points to the signs of the anointed one’s time and leaves John to draw the conclusion — and showing the honoured Baptist in doubt is a rough edge a hero-polisher would be unlikely to add.

objections.front: Parallelomania — the objection, and the reply.
objections.back: The objection (named by Samuel Sandmel, 1961): you can find patterns anywhere, and a method that can prove anything proves nothing. The reply: grant the observation, deny the inference — a method that finds Jesus everywhere has found him nowhere in particular, which is why responsible reading uses controls (the types the New Testament itself draws; correspondence plus escalation; organic fit in one story). We flag which readings are apostolic and which are later devotion, and lean on the former.

objections.front: The Hosea test case — why is Matthew not quote-mining?
objections.back: The objection is right about Hosea's grammar (past tense, 'son' = Israel) and wrong about Matthew's claim. 'Fulfill' is wider than prediction; the 'son' is Israel (Exodus 4:22) which is why Matthew chose it — he tells Jesus' early life as Israel's story walked again, faithful where Israel faltered; and Hosea 11 itself closes with a promised return (11:10–11), so Israel's own prophets already read the first exodus as the pattern of a greater one.

objections.front: Why is 'fulfill' (plēroō) wider than 'predict'?
objections.back: The New Testament uses 'fulfill' in more than one sense, not always to mean 'a prediction came true.' Often it means 'filled full': an earlier pattern reaches its completion in Christ. Jesus came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to 'fulfill' them (Matthew 5:17) — and commandments are not predictions. So a verse about Israel's past can be 'fulfilled' without being mistaken for a forecast.

objections.front: Why is the direct-prediction case handled in a different essay?
objections.back: Because 'direct prediction' (a forward-looking forecast checked against an event, like Micah 5:2 on Bethlehem) is only one of the four categories here, and the full case for it is the business of the companion essay on messianic prophecy. This essay's job is the method itself — that the New Testament sorts its citations and reads in context — not the forward-looking predictions.

objections.front: Why is “presupposed, never argued” stronger evidence than an argument would be?
objections.back: Because a thing presupposed offhandedly by a writer making some other point was not up for debate. Paul writes to settle other questions — a collection, a quarrel, a word of comfort — and assumes Christ’s divine status as common ground. The pattern runs through the undisputed letters, so it does not stand or fall with Colossians.

objections.front: Why is the persecutor the inventor thesis’s hardest witness?
objections.back: Because the reversal puts the causation backwards. He had violently persecuted the church for this belief — a crucified Messiah was a scandal, a hanged man under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23). You do not invent, at the cost of everything, the very belief you had been trying to stamp out. He did not build the confession; he joined it.

objections.front: “Nero didn’t even really target Christians, so the whole thing is inflated from the start.”
objections.back: Concede the disputed edge: some historians doubt the fire episode of 64 targeted Christians as Christians so early, others defend it, and both accept the Tacitus passage is genuine. But do not rest the case there. The firmer ground is Pliny onward, from about 112, and there the pattern is not in dispute — the datable core holds.

objections.front: “people die for false beliefs all the time — so martyrdom proves nothing.”
objections.back: Granted, and say it plainly: dying for a belief proves sincerity, not truth. But it does prove something worth having — it rules out cynical pretence, because you do not go to the beasts to keep up an act, especially when a pinch of incense would set you free. So these Christians genuinely believed Jesus was risen and Lord. Whether that belief is true is a sharper, separate question that belongs with the resurrection evidence.

objections.front: “Rome was only prosecuting disloyalty, not persecuting a religion.”
objections.back: Answered by the documents themselves: Pliny asked whether “the name itself” was the crime, Trajan’s answer in effect made it so, and anyone who would sacrifice and curse Christ walked free. Whatever Rome called the proceedings, the one thing that sent these people to their deaths was refusing to deny Christ.

objections.front: Why could every martyr have walked free — and why does that matter to the argument?
objections.back: Because the offence was the name itself: Pliny released everyone who sacrificed, prayed to the gods, and cursed Christ, and Trajan’s policy made anonymous hunting out of bounds. It matters because it rules out the manhunt story. These were not victims who could not escape; they were people handed an exit and refusing it — which is exactly why cynical pretence is the worst explanation of their deaths.

objections.front: “A secular humanist can just believe in progress on their own terms.” What is conceded, and what is the narrower tension?
objections.back: They can, and many do — the long-run data on declining violence and rising health are real and worth taking seriously; this track disputes not a line of them. The tension is narrower: an arc has to bend toward something, and a measurement of where we have gone cannot say which direction counts as forward. That needs a fixed point above history — which is exactly what the idea was born believing in.

objections.front: “Christians were often on the wrong side of the reforms you claim.” What is granted, and what is the point’s actual lane?
objections.back: Granted, without softening it: Christians have repeatedly stood on the wrong side of the very reforms this hope demands, defending what later Christians, reading the same Scriptures, would fight to abolish. But the point is genealogical, not congratulatory. That the source seeded the idea is compatible with those who carried it failing it, often and badly; the claim is that the belief history CAN bend toward justice is an inheritance, not a self-evident fact.

objections.front: “The Greeks and Romans believed in progress too.” Concede what, deny what?
objections.back: Concede it: the ancients did have technical and cultural notions of progress. But that is not the idea being traced. What the dominant ancient pictures lacked is the further conviction — that history as a whole is a story with a plot, morally judged, headed toward a goal it has not yet reached. That load-bearing picture came into the West through the biblical narrative, to which the critic who raised the objection himself gives a central place.

objections.front: “This is just Löwith’s secularization thesis, and Blumenberg refuted it.” What narrower claim survives?
objections.back: Concede the strong thesis is contested, and do not lean on it — the rebuttal that progress grows from within history is serious, and this track does not endorse the stronger secularization claim. But the point here is narrower, and it survives: what both sides actually share, and what is not seriously disputed, is that the biblical narrative made a distinctive, load-bearing contribution — time as a line with a moral destination, which the cyclical and declining images did not supply.

objections.front: How do you answer Ehrman — “early devotion is not the same as the Nicene dogma”?
objections.back: Concede first: the conceptual apparatus is later than Paul, the coherence of “one being, three persons” is still debated (though no contradiction has been demonstrated), and no single verse states it whole. But the data run the wrong way for a smooth upward evolution — the highest devotion sits in the earliest stratum, among Aramaic-speaking Jewish monotheists, within the first two decades. The councils did not add deity to a human Jesus; they supplied a grammar for the threeness and oneness the church had been confessing all along.

objections.front: How do you answer the unitarian reading of 1 Corinthians 8:6 — “one God” for the Father, the lesser title “Lord” for Jesus?
objections.back: Kyrios is the Septuagint’s rendering of the divine name itself. If “one Lord” means a being who is not the one God, then Paul has confessed, in an anti-idolatry argument, one God plus one divine-but-not-God Lord through whom all things were made — not the strict monotheism the objection wants. And creating marks the absolute line between God and everything else (“I am the LORD, who made all things,” Isaiah 44:24): the one through whom all things were made cannot be among the things made. The reading keeps “one God, the Father” only by making “one Lord” say less than it says.

objections.front: What genuinely DID develop — and why does conceding it not concede the invention thesis?
objections.back: The apparatus of ousia and hypostasis is later than Paul; no single verse states the doctrine whole. Nicaea’s own word, homoousios, was so far from an instant slogan that for nearly twenty years scarcely anyone invoked it, and the decades after 325 were a chaos of competing parties; the full ousia/hypostaseis synthesis was the Cappadocians’, and the fuller clause on the Spirit came from Constantinople (381). Grant all of it. What the concession does not touch is the “invention” thesis: the doctrine those terms protect — the Son fully God and not a creature, worshipped alongside the Father, the one God somehow Father, Son, and Spirit — is the very thing Paul’s worship already presupposed.

objections.front: Why does Paul’s reworking of the Shema sharpen monotheism rather than add a second god?
objections.back: Because he does it inside a jealous monotheism: “there is no God but one” (1 Corinthians 8:4), and in the next breath “one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:6). On N. T. Wright’s much-discussed reading, Paul distributes Israel’s one confession of the one Lord God between the Father and Jesus — expanding the Shema from within to include the Son, not adding a second god. That is monotheism sharpened, not softened — the reading is influential, arguably dominant, and genuinely contested.

objections.front: “It grew fast, so it must be true.” What is the reply — and why is this the one that matters most?
objections.back: This one cuts against us, and we grant it in our own voice: growth is not truth. People risk much for beliefs that turn out false, and fast growth is not unique to Christianity — Stark observed his rate is close to the twentieth-century growth of the Latter-day Saints, a curve of the same shape. The rise shows the movement was compelling and costly to join; whether its central claim is true rests on the resurrection, argued elsewhere. The argument’s job is the narrower one: to refute the claim that the state did it.

objections.front: Why does Galerius’s edict of 311 matter to the timing of the argument?
objections.back: Because it shows the state conceded first. Decius’s order of 250, Valerian’s edicts of 257–58 and Diocletian’s persecution from 303 were all spent, and the last was formally abandoned by Galerius in the edict of toleration of April 311 — a full year before the Milvian Bridge of 312. So Constantine did not create the movement; the state gave up fighting one that had already grown while completely illegal.

objections.front: Why does the Constantine objection explain “the wrong stretch of the curve”?
objections.back: Concede the fourth century entirely: after 312 everything is entangled with state power and the majority was reached under that thumb, so the AD 400 majority is not evidence of persuasive force. But Pliny, Lucian and Cornelius all predate Constantine, and two persecutions had already failed. By the time Constantine acted the church already numbered in the millions; his patronage recognised a movement already too big to suppress — for the stretch before 312 the objection reverses cause and effect.

objections.front: Why is Keith Hopkins NOT independent confirmation of the high figure?
objections.back: Because he takes Stark’s arithmetic as his starting point — he adopts Stark’s endpoints and rate rather than reaching an independent estimate, and his contribution is to probe what such totals imply about community size and structure. He is therefore corroboration of Stark’s method, not of his conclusion, so he cannot be cited as an independent second voice for the numbers.

objections.front: Why is Stark’s figure “a model, not a census,” and does the case rest on it?
objections.back: There was never any count of Christians in the empire; every figure is an estimate built from fragments, and Stark said his table is a model generated from an assumed constant rate. It cannot even be extended past the mid-fourth century without exceeding the empire’s population. That is why the honest answer is a range — roughly 2.5 to 6.3 million by 300 — and why the case does not rest on the numbers at all, but on the datable, hostile, pre-Constantinian evidence that a large organised movement already existed.

objections.front: “‘Science was born from Christianity’ is just the warfare myth flipped over.”
objections.back: Agreed, and the track states it in its own voice: historians resist any monocausal story, and “that Christianity gave birth to modern science” is itself counted among the myths a leading volume dismantles. Take it as the careful historians offer it — theological preconditions that made the enterprise thinkable and durable, a contested interpretation, not a demonstrated law of history.

objections.front: “Science was really a Greek and Islamic achievement, not a Christian one.”
objections.back: All true, and the case needs no Christian monopoly. Science stands on Greek mathematics and logic and on the Islamic Golden Age — Ibn al-Haytham’s optics pioneered controlled experiment centuries before Europe. The careful thesis is only that Christian convictions about a rational, contingent, intelligible creation were the fertile soil in which the self-sustaining enterprise took decisive root in early-modern Europe — offered alongside those debts, never against them.

objections.front: “They were all believers only because everyone in Europe was baptised.”
objections.back: Granted — in a Europe where nearly everyone was baptised, the founders being members of the church would prove little on its own. What matters is not their membership but that so many of them said, in their own writings, that faith was their reason for looking.

objections.front: Who retired the warfare thesis — and why does that matter to the argument?
objections.back: The mainstream of the discipline retired it, many of them with no religious stake at all. That matters because the correction is not a fringe Christian complaint but the settled verdict of secular and believing historians alike — which is exactly what makes it worth trusting.

objections.front: Why doesn’t the Galileo affair prove a war between faith and science?
objections.back: Concede the injustice fully first: the Roman authorities were wrong to condemn him and wrong to bind Scripture to one astronomy. But in 1616 the evidence did not yet favour Copernicus — his system used circles and epicycles and predicted no better than Ptolemy, and Tycho’s system kept the earth still while fitting the same data, including the phases of Venus. The dispute cut across both church and academy. One tragedy is not a three-century war.

objections.front: “The strongest worship scenes are in the latest books” — why does that not rescue a slow development?
objections.back: Because the case rests its weight on the earliest material, not the latest: a pre-Pauline Aramaic prayer from the Jerusalem church of the 30s, a hymn widely regarded as older than the letter that carries it, and Paul’s undisputed letters of the 50s defining the church as those who “call upon the name” of Jesus. Revelation and John make the worship vivid; they did not invent it.

objections.front: Why does the angel’s refusal in Revelation matter so much?
objections.back: It is the control case. Even the highest created messenger refuses the worship due God alone, which tells us precisely what the earliest Christians thought they were — and were not — free to do. And in the same book the Lamb receives the same blessing and honour and glory as the one on the throne: the Lamb receives what the angel forbids.

objections.front: Why is Marana tha the strongest single piece of evidence for an EARLY date?
objections.back: Because it is Aramaic — a fossil of devotion in the original language of the Palestinian church, preserved untranslated in Paul’s Greek. It carries us behind Paul to the first Aramaic-speaking believers in Jerusalem in the 30s. The most explosive evidence is also the earliest.

objections.front: Consciousness is just brain activity.
objections.back: Correlation is not explanation. We can map which neurons fire when you see red - the easy problem - but why is that firing felt rather than happening in the dark? Describe the whole mechanism and you can still ask: why is it like something?

objections.front: Consciousness is just emergence, like wetness.
objections.back: Wetness is weakly emergent - explicable from molecules. Consciousness is strongly emergent - the parts give no clue why experience appears. "Emergent" names the mystery, not the solution.

objections.front: The strongest objection: Chalmers and Nagel aren’t theists.
objections.back: Granting the hard problem is real does not entail God. Chalmers prefers naturalistic dualism; Nagel (atheist) a non-theistic teleology. The failure of materialism opens a space theism shares with panpsychism and naturalistic dualism.

objections.front: Why does consciousness fit theism better than naturalism?
objections.back: On naturalism you must get mind from mindless matter (the hard problem). On theism you start with Mind, and finite minds are exactly what a conscious Creator would produce.

objections.front: It’s just an evolutionary byproduct.
objections.back: Not refutation but a question of adequacy: evolution explains why we keep striving, but less clearly the SHAPE of Joy - a homesickness for a place never been, that intensifies when every earthly good is secured. A survival instinct satisfied by nothing attainable is a strange one. A clue, not a proof.

objections.front: Wanting something doesn’t make it exist.
objections.back: Grant it at once - any defender treating this as a proof has overreached. Lewis said "most probable explanation," not a demonstration; it is abductive and cumulative. Many impossible desires (to fly, to live forever) are a real good aimed at an impossible mode.

objections.front: What is Beversluis’s circularity charge, and how do you answer it?
objections.back: A desire counts as "natural" only if it has a real object - the very thing to be proved - so the inconvenient cases get filed under "artificial." The honest answer CONCEDES the distinction is not load-bearing ("spontaneous and universal" is not "has a real object"; the desire never to die looks natural yet has no object in this life) and shifts the case to the shape of Joy.

objections.front: Where does the honest case really rest - and why not on the natural/artificial distinction?
objections.back: On the phenomenological surplus - the peculiar shape of Joy - because the natural/artificial distinction draws a fair circularity charge and cannot be made load-bearing. The major premise is a contested hinge no neutral instrument settles.

objections.argName: The Problem of Evil as Evidence for God
objections.front: What is the hardest objection, and how do you answer it?
objections.back: The EVIDENTIAL problem (Rowe): the amount of apparently gratuitous suffering is evidence AGAINST God. Concede its force - it is live and unresolved. But it and the turnabout are about different things: one asks if this much suffering fits God, the other asks what it means to call it evil at all. Both can stand.

objections.argName: The Problem of Evil as Evidence for God
objections.front: What is the is/ought gap, and why does it matter?
objections.back: From a complete description of what IS, no verdict about what OUGHT to be follows by logic alone. "This hurts" is not yet "this is wrong." The wrongness is a standard laid over the facts - and that standard is what the argument points at.

objections.front: "A final theory will show the constants had to be this way" — reply?
objections.back: A promissory note, not present physics. And it would have to be the right theory out of countless possible law-structures — a staggering coincidence that the one necessary set also permits life. The tuning moves up to the laws; it doesn’t vanish.

objections.front: What is the firing-squad reply to "we couldn’t observe otherwise"?
objections.back: Fifty marksmen all miss: either the guns held blanks (design), you witnessed a fluke (chance), or there were countless firing squads — the multiverse again, with its own unpaid bills. Observer selection explains why we see a survivable outcome, not why there is one.

objections.front: Why does the multiverse not cleanly defeat fine-tuning?
objections.back: It is unobserved with no agreed observational test; the mechanism that would generate it seems to need its own fine-tuning; and in many models freak Boltzmann-brain observers outnumber observers like us. The problem is pushed back, not erased.

objections.front: Why is A Fortunate Universe worth citing?
objections.back: It is co-written by two astrophysicists who agree on the data and divide on its meaning — Geraint Lewis reads it as a multiverse, Luke Barnes as a designer. Proof the data is cross-worldview, not apologetics.

objections.front: "Mathematicians use infinities fine (Cantor)" — reply?
objections.back: Coherent as a mathematical concept is not the same as instantiable as a concrete collection in the physical world. Hilbert’s Hotel is counterintuitive, not contradictory — so the claim narrows to concrete instantiation, and whether THAT holds is the disputed hinge.

objections.front: Morriston’s objection to Premise 1 — and the reply?
objections.back: Our causal sense is built from events inside time, so why extend it to the beginning of time itself? Reply: the principle rests on a metaphysical insight about being and non-being (nothing has no powers, so it can produce nothing), not mere induction.

objections.front: "Quantum particles come from nothing" — reply?
objections.back: The quantum vacuum is not nothing — it’s structured energy governed by laws; a particle from it is like a wave from the ocean. An indeterministic event isn’t uncaused, and "out of nothing" denies a material cause, not an efficient one.

objections.front: State Premise 1 — and why not "everything has a cause"?
objections.back: Whatever BEGINS to exist has a cause. Not "everything" — that invites "then what caused the cause?" The restriction to things that begin is principled, built in from the start.

objections.front: "Then isn’t God infinitely old?" — reply?
objections.back: The arguments target a physical series of events; on the classical account God’s eternity is not a series of moments at all, so there is nothing to "complete." Don’t call God "infinitely old." Christians differ on how God relates to time; the Kalam settles none of it.

objections.front: "What caused God?" — reply?
objections.back: P1 is only about things that begin to exist. God never began, so He falls outside a rule that was about beginnings all along — principled, not special pleading. Like asking what the bachelor’s wife is doing tonight.

objections.front: Why must the cause be personal, not a mechanism?
objections.back: Timeless/spaceless/immaterial — so an abstract object or an unembodied mind; abstracts cause nothing. And a changeless cause with a temporal effect is best explained by a free act of will (agent causation). Inference to the best explanation, not proof.

objections.front: Explaining each part explains the whole.
objections.back: Why this chain rather than none? A whole composed entirely of contingent things, with no necessary member anywhere in it, has nothing within it that grounds its existence.

objections.front: How does "explanation by free choice" answer modal collapse?
objections.back: The explanans (God) is necessary, but the explaining ACT is free - a free agent could have chosen otherwise - so the world is explained without being necessitated. It leans on a libertarian view of free will, which is itself contested.

objections.front: Reply to the taxicab objection: the theist uses the PSR, then dismisses it at God.
objections.back: Premise 1 never said everything has an external cause; God satisfies the principle as the being whose explanation lies in his own necessary nature. The taxi is not dismissed; it arrives at its proper destination.

objections.front: The universe is just a brute fact.
objections.back: A brute initial state explains nothing about why it obtains, while a necessary ground that freely chooses to create explains both that there is a world and why it is contingent. "The universe is just there" is a possible answer but not the better one.

objections.front: Why isn’t the universe itself the necessary being?
objections.back: It doesn’t look necessary: we can readily conceive it with different laws, different particles, or not at all. A being whose every part could have been different is a poor candidate for existing by the sheer necessity of its own nature.

objections.front: Why must the necessary being be more than a number?
objections.back: Abstract objects are causally impotent - a number cannot cause a universe. The ground of contingent reality must be able to cause, and plausibly chooses - so it is plausibly a mind, not an inert abstraction.

objections.front: Why doesn’t evolution ground morality?
objections.back: It may explain why we have moral beliefs, not whether any are true. If ought is just a survival trick it has no binding authority - that debunks morality rather than grounds it.

objections.front: How do you answer the reverse/symmetry parody?
objections.back: The two claims are not perfectly symmetric: maximal greatness is a positive, coherent concept whose impossibility would need a hidden contradiction no one has produced. In our judgment that tilts the scales; it does not compel. And the atheist must now hold God is impossible, not merely absent.

objections.front: How does the modal version answer Kant?
objections.back: Against any form that treats bare existence as one more perfection, Kant’s objection has real force. The modal version shifts the ground to NECESSARY existence as a modal property - though whether it fully escapes Kant is itself debated.

objections.front: What is the strongest objection (the reverse parody)?
objections.back: "Possibly, NO maximally great being exists" - which in S5 would make God impossible. It shows the argument cannot coerce: it is only as strong as the possibility premise, and the mirror looks like an epistemic par.

objections.front: You’re just defining God into existence.
objections.back: It does not define God as existing; it argues that IF a necessary being is even possible, the modal logic entails its actuality - a substantive result, not a stipulation. The real action is the open metaphysical possibility premise.

objections.front: Anscombe’s 1948 objection - and how Lewis answered it.
objections.back: A merely non-rational cause of a belief is not an irrational one; a full causal history does not by itself impugn validity. Lewis took it seriously and substantially revised the chapter (1960) around the cause/ground distinction - the version in view today.

objections.front: Evolution selects for true beliefs.
objections.back: Grant that behaviour is adaptive. On naturalism a belief causes behaviour through its neurophysiology, not its meaning, so many false belief-contents yield the same behaviour. Naturalism has not yet shown how content-blind selection yields truth-tracking minds.

objections.front: Reasons just are physical causes.
objections.back: If the physical level does all the causal work, the rational level is epiphenomenal - along for the ride, doing nothing. Then you hold a conclusion because of neural causes, and truth drops out of the explanation - which is exactly the problem.

objections.front: Why isn’t this "self-refuting"?
objections.back: It does not say reason is unreliable. It says the naturalist cannot, without strain, both explain reason as a byproduct of non-rational causes and rely on it. The conclusion is to reject naturalism, not reason - it targets naturalism, not rationality.

objections.front: Alston’s parity proves too much (astrology could claim it too).
objections.back: Christian Mystical Practice has internal overriders (a spirit contradicting Scripture is suspect) and a coherent object; astrology has neither, nor a morally transforming self-correcting tradition. The debate continues, and it is genuinely unsettled.

objections.front: Different religions contradict (the hardest objection).
objections.back: It LIMITS the argument, it does not kill it. The reports conflict over WHAT was encountered, so experience alone cannot settle which God is real. What survives is only the thin claim that many met something beyond the physical - a shared report, not a shared object. It leaves the experiencer’s own warrant largely intact while sharply reducing public-proof force.

objections.front: How does Hick try to answer the diversity problem, and what is the cost?
objections.back: Hick proposes one ineffable "Real" refracted through every tradition’s lens. The cost: it requires saying no tradition perceives the Real as it is - which cannot be squared with the Christian claim that God has made himself known in Christ (John 1:18; 14:9).

objections.front: It is just brain chemistry (the "God helmet").
objections.back: Every experience has a neural correlate - seeing a tree lights up the visual cortex too - so a brain-state does not make it a hallucination; "it is in the brain, so only the brain" is a reductionist fallacy. And the God-helmet failed replication: a 2005 Swedish double-blind (Granqvist) found the field made no difference, suggestibility did, using Persinger’s own equipment.

objections.front: It is just wish-fulfillment (Freud).
objections.back: Pressed to a verdict about truth it is a genetic fallacy - wanting a belief does not make it false. And much religious experience is UNWELCOME (conviction of sin, Isaiah’s "Woe is me," a consuming fire), a poor fit for comfort-projection. Partial value, overreaches as a universal solvent.

objections.front: What is Alston’s "doxastic practice," and why does it matter?
objections.back: A socially established, self-monitoring way of forming beliefs with internal checks - like sense perception or memory. None can be shown reliable without circularity, yet all are rational to use. Alston argues Christian Mystical Practice is structurally just another one.

objections.front: Why is the Principle of Credulity asymmetric?
objections.back: If you seem to experience God, that counts for God; but failing to experience God does NOT count against him. Absence of the experience is not evidence of absence.

objections.front: Oppy’s challenge - why not a necessary physical state?
objections.back: A brute necessary physical state is composite and changeable, so it still has potency to be actualized - it fails the very test that forced us up the series. Only something purely actual and absolutely simple can be the terminus. Whether the cosmos could be that is the live crux.

objections.front: Potency and act - why must whatever changes be changed by another?
objections.back: Change is a potential becoming actual. A potential cannot actualize itself (cold water does not heat itself); something already actual must do it. Trace the present chain of actualizers to its source.

objections.front: Why can the per se series not be infinite?
objections.back: Its later members are mere instruments with no power of their own. An infinite series of instruments with no first source explains nothing - like an endless paintbrush with no painter.

objections.front: Why is this not just the Kalam?
objections.back: Kalam is about a temporal beginning. The Thomistic argument is about here-and-now dependence - what sustains things in existence right now, even if the universe were eternal. Aquinas held reason cannot even prove the universe began.

objections.front: Why must the First Cause be only one?
objections.back: Two purely actual beings would have to differ, and difference requires one to have some potency or limitation the other lacks - contradicting pure actuality. So there is only one. (This is the oneness of the divine nature, not a denial of the Trinity.)

objections.front: “Collins says the numbers are simply inexact” — why does that cut both ways?
objections.back: If the author of a Maccabean Daniel was writing about events in his own lifetime, his inability to make 490 years reach cleanly from any starting point to 164 BC is itself a little awkward — he, of all people, knew when Antiochus desecrated the temple. The looseness is real, but it equally undermines any tidy this-equals-that Maccabean fulfillment.

objections.front: Why does the Maccabean reading fit a clause but not the whole?
objections.back: After Onias III’s death the city was sacked in part and the sanctuary profaned, but the sanctuary itself was not destroyed and was rededicated (1 Maccabees 4:52–54). Daniel’s terminal event is that the people of the prince “shall destroy the city and the sanctuary” — which happened only after Jesus’s death, in AD 70.

objections.front: The creed says Jesus appeared “to the twelve,” but only eleven were left.
objections.back: A category mistake: “the Twelve” is not a running head-count but the fixed name of the apostolic body, used even where it cannot mean twelve people; the Gospels say “the eleven” precisely when eleven is meant. A deliberate institutional label, not a slip of the tally — the mainstream reading, though a determined skeptic may still call the title idealized.

objections.front: Why does Paul’s fifteen-day visit to Jerusalem matter to the date?
objections.back: The verb Paul uses connotes inquiry — getting to know a person and, plausibly, his account — and the two men he names there are precisely two of the named recipients of appearances in the creed. Whether he received the formula at his conversion or had it confirmed in that fortnight, it predates his receipt of it.

objections.front: Why does the pair “delivered … received” matter?
objections.back: It is the precise idiom used in Judaism for the transmission of authoritative tradition. Paul is not narrating his own experience here; he is handing on something handed to him.

objections.front: Why does the shape of the lines count as evidence?
objections.back: Balanced clauses, each introduced by hoti (“that”), in a fourfold rhythm — died, was buried, was raised, appeared — read as a confession to be memorized rather than prose to be composed on the fly.

objections.front: Why is the five-hundred report, found only in Paul, not a weakness?
objections.back: The five hundred are reported only by Paul, not in the Gospels; but Paul’s closeness to the tradition — he had met its named witnesses — is precisely the point, not a weakness. And the early-dating argument never leaned on them.

objections.front: But Jesus grows, prays, and does not know the hour.
objections.back: The New Testament holds both halves on purpose, often in one breath — the upholder of the universe “made purification for sins” (Heb. 1:3). The counter-lines describe what the Son took on; the HANDS lines describe what he never ceased to be.

objections.front: Sitting at God’s right hand means NOT being God.
objections.back: Two persons, certainly — that is Trinitarianism, not a problem for it. A viceroy may be seated beside a king, and by the king’s grant may even share his rule; what no viceroy receives is that worship. Revelation pictures one throne of God and of the Lamb, before which the redeemed render undivided worship.

objections.front: The developmental objection — what does it say developed, and what answers it?
objections.back: It claims two lines of development: in exaltation Christologies the moment Jesus became Son was pushed back from resurrection to baptism to birth; in incarnation Christologies what developed was not the date of pre-existence but the pre-existent figure’s rank — conceived at first as a subordinate divine being, whose elevation to the co-equal God is the later step. Answer: the earliest worship already placed Jesus inside the one God’s identity, not beneath it as a lesser divinity. No Jewish writer we know of wrote a second figure into the creed of divine uniqueness itself (Philo’s “second god,” the Logos, is the nearest case, and it is never placed inside that confession); Paul did — on a reading of 1 Corinthians 8:6 that is influential and genuinely contested. So at the point that matters, we judge that the developmental thesis does not hold.

objections.front: Why does agency have a ceiling — and where is it?
objections.back: No shaliach in Jewish thought ever received the cultic worship — offered to God, alongside God — that the New Testament gives Jesus; agency conferred authority, not that adoration. Grant that God’s name and authority could be entrusted to a supreme agent; the worship still could not be, and, on the divine-identity reading, neither could the work of creation.

objections.front: Why does the worship in Revelation carry weight?
objections.back: Every creature sings “to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb” the same blessing and honor, and the elders fall down and worship — though the same book twice has an angel refuse worship with “Worship God!” The Lamb receives what the angel forbids.

objections.front: Josephus’s earlier history of the war never mentions Jesus.
objections.back: That book is a history of the revolt and the political road to it; what earns a mention there is bearing on the conflict, not bare existence. His later, sprawling history of the whole Jewish people is where he pauses over religious figures at the edges of the main story, John the Baptist among them. The omission is a fact about a book’s scope, not evidence that there was no one to omit.

objections.front: Paul says almost nothing about the earthly Jesus.
objections.back: The inference mistakes the kind of documents these are: occasional letters to congregations he had already taught in person, which presuppose the story of Jesus rather than retell it. And the silence is not total: born of woman, born under the law, descended from David according to the flesh, a last supper on the night he was betrayed, crucified and buried — a spare but recognizably earthly outline.

objections.front: Tacitus just repeated what Christians told him.
objections.back: This is widely treated as independent of Christian sources — though some scholars suspect Tacitus may be relaying what Christians of his own day reported — and either way it shows a hostile Roman writer took the bedrock fact for granted: a man called Christ was executed under Pilate.

objections.front: Why does Paul’s remark about “the Lord’s brother” carry such weight?
objections.back: It is the testimony of a man who was at first a persecutor of the church, who had no motive to fabricate, and who is writing to people who could have checked his claims. If Jesus had been a purely celestial being who never walked the earth, it is exceedingly strange that his contemporaries should include a man universally known as his brother, whom Paul says he met face to face.

objections.front: Why is the silence of the ancient critics evidence?
objections.back: Jesus had determined enemies — pagan critics like Celsus and a hostile strand of Jewish polemic — who charged sorcery, deception, and illegitimate birth. What no ancient opponent is known to have argued is that there had been no such man at all. They argued about what he was, not whether he was.

objections.argName: Jesus as God in the New Testament
objections.front: The baptism voice and “declared Son by his resurrection” show he was adopted.
objections.back: That is a reconstruction of a layer behind the texts, genuinely debated; the texts as we have them do not require it. The one “declared with power to be the Son of God by his resurrection” is already “His Son, who was a descendant of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3–4). The contrast is between the Son in the weakness of the flesh and the Son in power, not between a mere man and an adopted Son. A confirmation needs something to confirm.

objections.argName: Jesus as God in the New Testament
objections.front: The “God” texts all depend on disputed grammar.
objections.back: Candor costs the case nothing. Grant every concession on the contested three and two direct predications still stand — John’s confession, which no grammatical alternative touches, and Hebrews’ “O God,” which rests on the reading its own chapter’s argument favours. The disputed grammar is the weakest leg, not the foundation; the weight falls on worship and divine identity.

objections.argName: Jesus as God in the New Testament
objections.front: Why does an Aramaic two-word prayer in a Greek letter matter?
objections.back: That the invocation survives untranslated carries us back behind Paul’s Greek to the Aramaic-speaking Judean church, calling on the risen Jesus as the Lord who will come. It is prayer, not the homage due a vice-regent — the highest devotion is bedrock, not a late Hellenistic overlay.

objections.argName: Jesus as God in the New Testament
objections.front: Why does the “every knee shall bow” line in the Philippians hymn carry so much weight?
objections.back: It is lifted from a passage where the LORD swears that to him alone every knee shall bow — and Paul applies it to Jesus. A text reserved for the one God is given, by a monotheist Jew, to Jesus.

objections.argName: Jesus as God in the New Testament
objections.front: Why does Thomas’s “My Lord and my God” form a floor no grammar dispute touches?
objections.back: The narrator frames the words as spoken to Jesus (“said to him”); the phrase functions as a vocative of direct address; and Jesus accepts the confession and blesses those who will believe without seeing, while John lets it stand as the climax of the book.

objections.argName: Did Jesus Claim to Be God
objections.front: Why does the forgiveness of sins carry weight?
objections.back: A person could declare that God had forgiven someone, or pronounce forgiveness within the Temple system; Jesus bypasses Temple, priesthood, and sacrifice and forgives on his own authority. The scribes’ premise that only God forgives is theologically correct, and he acts inside it. The one counter-example urged is too textually broken to settle the point and, at most, describes mediated agency.

objections.front: The argument is circular — the same Gospels supply both the claims and the character.
objections.back: It need not treat the Gospels as uniformly reliable or wholly unreliable. On ordinary critical grounds the broad moral character and the implicit authority-claims are well-rooted in the tradition, while specific Johannine formulations get more caution; the argument takes what critical scholarship grants and asks what best explains it — layered, not viciously circular.

objections.front: Why does the sinlessness claim carry weight?
objections.back: The earliest Christians make it about Jesus and about no one else, and ancient literature almost never makes it about anyone. And it was rendered not by distant admirers but by Jews steeped in a tradition that insisted all have sinned.

objections.front: Why is ‘a great moral teacher, but not God’ not an option?
objections.back: Because such claims cannot be made innocently: a morally good and mentally sound human being does not go about implying that he is the hinge of history, standing where only God stands. The character and the claims come as a package, and the package will not be unwrapped.

objections.front: Why is the ‘lunatic’ horn improbable — and what must the defender concede?
objections.back: A man who diagnosed self-deception in others with surgical precision would have to be catastrophically self-deceived at the centre of his self-understanding, with no other mark on a life his intimates judged blameless. Concede: grandiosity and sanctity have, on rare occasions, coexisted.

objections.argName: John 1:1 and the Pre-existence of Christ
objections.front: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28) shows the Word is a lesser, derived god.
objections.back: The Son’s subordination in John is functional (in his role and incarnation), not ontological (in his nature). The words are spoken by the Son who has taken “the form of a servant,” having been “in the form of God” (Philippians 2:6–7): the Father is greater in position, within the incarnate mission, not greater in deity. The Son is not lesser in being, made, or later than the Father — co-equal and co-eternal, sharing one divine nature.

objections.argName: John 1:1 and the Pre-existence of Christ
objections.front: The Greek has no article, so it says “a god.”
objections.back: The absence of the article does not by itself make a noun indefinite; this construction points to quality, not indefiniteness. The grammar ascribes the kind; the monotheism of the same Gospel, which knows only one divine nature and no gradations within the Godhead, rules out any lesser deity. The technical form of the argument takes a qualitative reading and then translates it indefinitely — a further step, and one the study’s own paraphrase does not take. The article-less theos does mark a distinction — the Word is not the Father — but between two persons sharing one divine nature, not between God and a demigod.

objections.front: The evangelists wrote the details in to match the texts.
objections.back: Concede it for the stageable prophecies.
